ch06.note: 'The bandits' (匪, or 共匪 'Communist bandits') is the standard Nationalist name for the Chinese Communists and their armies. It recurs throughout the book—'bandit-suppression,' 'the bandit areas,' 'the bandit chief Mao'—and is always political, never a reference to ordinary outlaws.

Having lost the civil war, Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government withdrew to the island of Taiwan in 1949 and ruled from Taipei; the mainland became the People's Republic under the Communists. Chen writes from Taiwan decades later, so the book's 'now' is Taiwan and its 'then' the mainland; 'the late President' is Chiang, who died there in 1975.

Mount Lu (庐山, Lushan), a cool highland resort in Jiangxi, served as Chiang Kai-shek's summer headquarters, where officials came for audiences and where he convened important conferences. To be received 'at Nanjing and Mount Lu' meant access to the seat of power in both its winter and summer homes.

Zhongnanhai (中南海), the 'Central and Southern Seas,' a walled compound of lakes and gardens immediately west of the old Forbidden City in Beijing, long used as a seat of government; it is today the headquarters of China's Communist leadership.

ch06.anchor: also a fellow provincial from Sichuan
ch06.note: Shared native place (同乡, tongxiang—the same province, county, or town) created one of the strongest bonds of trust and mutual obligation in Chinese life, opening doors that were closed to strangers. Chen notes such ties throughout as the hidden grain along which loyalty and recruitment ran.

ch06.anchor: ranked with Li Dazhao and Chen Duxiu
ch06.note: Li Dazhao (李大钊, 1889–1927) and Chen Duxiu (陈独秀, 1879–1942), the two principal founders of the Chinese Communist Party in 1921; Chen was its first General Secretary, and Li was arrested and hanged at Beijing in 1927 by the warlord Zhang Zuolin. To be 'ranked with' them marks a man as a Communist of the first generation.

In April 1927 Chiang Kai-shek turned on the Communists who had been the Nationalists' allies, and in Shanghai and elsewhere they were rounded up and killed by the thousand—the 'party purge' (清党) or 'White Terror' that split the two parties and opened twenty-two years of intermittent civil war.

ch06.anchor: announced his retirement by open telegram
ch06.note: The open or 'circular telegram' (通电, tongdian) was a characteristic instrument of Republican politics: a public declaration wired at once to officials, newspapers, and rivals across the country, used to announce a resignation, denounce an enemy, or rally support. Several turns of this book hinge on one.

ch06.anchor: startle all with its first cry
ch06.note: An allusion to the proverb of the bird that sits silent for three years and then 'with a single cry startles everyone' (一鸣惊人)—of one who does nothing remarkable for a long while and then astonishes the world at a stroke. It is told of King Zhuang of Chu in the Han Feizi and of King Wei of Qi in Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian.

ch06.anchor: was struggled to death by the Chinese Communists
ch06.note: To be 'struggled' (斗, from 斗争/批斗) is to be subjected to a struggle session: a public mass denunciation in which the accused is harangued, humiliated, and often beaten, a signature method of Communist campaigns and especially of the Cultural Revolution (1966–76). Many of Chen's contemporaries met their end this way.

Chinese families ranked children by order of birth, and a person—here a woman—could be known simply by surname plus that number, 'Zhu the Ninth' meaning the ninth-born of the Zhu children. The same reckoning underlies the many 'Third Master' and 'Fourth Brother' names in the book.

ch06.anchor: into the Northeast by a roundabout route, to organize a Volunteer Army
ch06.note: After Japan seized Manchuria in 1931, irregular 'Anti-Japanese Volunteer Armies' (义勇军) sprang up across the Northeast. General Li Du (李杜, 1880–1956) was a leader of this resistance, commanding the Jilin Self-Defense Army until, overwhelmed, he withdrew into the Soviet Union in 1933 and made his way back to China.
